cards.title: A. The French Wars of Religion (1562-1598)
body: It was fought between the Catholics and the Huguenots (French Protestants) for about 30 years. It only ended when Henry VI issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598, which recognized Catholicism as the official religion of France and allowed the Huguenots the right of worship.

cards.title: Causes
body: 1. French kings started persecuting Protestants to stop its spread.
2. The rise of the Huguenots, French Protestants influenced by John Calvin, mostly made up of the nobles who opposed the monarchial rule of the kings.
3. Competition between the Catholics and the Calvinists to acquire followers.

cards.title: B. Dutch-Spanish war (1566-1609)
body: King Philip II (1556-1598), the son of Charles V, brought political and cultural greatness in Spain. To consolidate his inheritance from his father (Spain, the Netherlands, Italy, and the Americas), he insisted on strict Catholicism and strong monarchial authority.

cards.title: Causes
body: 1. Philip II attempted to strengthen his rule by crushing Calvinism in the Netherlands (made up of 17 provinces).

2. Calvinist nobles of the Northern provinces attacked Catholic churches and statues in 1566. Philip sent 10,000 troops to crush the rebellion and fought until 1609. The war ended with a 12-year truce and the United Provinces of the Netherlands was created.

cards.title: C. Spanish-English naval war
body: Elizabeth Tudor (1558- 1603) led a protestant rule in England. She exercised a moderate foreign policy by shifting sides between Spain and France to prevent either of them from being too powerful. But King Philip of Spain had had a long term plan to invade England in order to;
1. Safeguard Spanish merchant ships and colonies in the Americas from British raids.
2. Depose the Protestant rule of Queen Elizabeth I.
3. Restore Catholicism in England
In 1588, Philip tried to invade England with the Spanish Armada (of more than 200 warships) but was defeated by the English navy in the English Channel with more than 100 of the ships destroyed.
The Spanish- English war created the shift of power from Spain to England and France.

lessons.title: War, Revolution and Socio-economic Crisis in the 16th C

cards.title: War, Revolution and Socio-economic Crisis in the 16th C
body: Europe during the 16th C faced many problems such as;

cards.title: A. Economic Problems (1560-1650)- Inflation (increase in prices) was caused by.
body: Influx (when the supply exceeds the demand) of gold and silver from the Americas
Rise of Population in the 16th C- it increased from 60 million in 1500 to 85 million in 1600.
1650 population decline in central and southern Europe due to Warfare, plague and famine.

cards.title: B. The Witchcraft Trials
body: New religious enthusiasm against the ancient beliefs of witchcraft and magic led to the Inquisition to hunt those who were believed to have practiced witchcraft.

Thousands of people were charged with witchcraft and almost 30,000 of them were executed by either burning of hanging. Those actions brought fear and disturbances in the European societies until the governments lost interest in the trials in around 1650.

cards.title: C. The Thirty Years’ War (1618-1648) – Causes
body: The spread of Calvinism all over Europe in the 1600s.

While recognizing Lutheranism in Germany, the Peace of Augsburg (1555) didn’t include Calvinism. The conflict between the Calvinists and the Catholic Church begun in Bohemia (Czech Republic) against the Hapsburg dynasty (Austria) and Holy Roman Empire. The revolution later spread into Denmark, Sweden, France, and Spain.

Most of the war was fought on German soil but the greatest human loss was in the Holy Roman Empire. The war ended in 1648 with the Peace of Westphalia allowing all German states to choose their own religions and it recognized the political independence of the 300 states within the Holy Roman Empire.
This became the end of the Empire and emergence of modern nation-states.

cards.title: D. English Revolutions in the 17th C – Causes
body: Disputes between the King and the Parliament arose after the death of Elizabeth I in 1603. The Stuart dynasty led by King James I of Scotland (Elizabeth’s cousin) rose to power in England. But his idea of divine rights of kings was rejected by the Parliament because they believed the King or Queen and the Parliament should rule together.
Puritans (English Protestants inspired by Calvinists) members of the House of Commons, wanted a separate church from the Catholic Church of England.

The English civil war of 1642 was fought between the Cavaliers or Royalists (the supporters of King Charles I, the son of James I) and the Roundheads (supporters of the Parliament), after Charles rejected of the Parliament’s petition against tax laws, because like his father, Charles believed in the divine rights of the kings.

The Parliament won the war led by Oliver Cromwell and Charles I was executed in 1649. Monarchy was abolished making England a Republic or a commonwealth. But after the death of Cromwell in 1658, the Monarchy was once again restored under the rule of Charles II (son of Charles I).

Charles’s brother James II was a devoted Catholic whose monarchial rule frightened the Parliament when his son was born, thus the English nobles invited Dutch Protestant leaders William and Mary to invade England in 1688. King James escaped to France; this revolution is known as the Glorious Revolution.

In 1689, Mary and William were crowned the Queen and King of England by the Parliament. They passed The Bill of Rights recognizing the Parliament’s rights to make laws and levy taxes. It replaced the divine right of kings by a government system based on the rule of law, a freely elected Parliament, and limited Constitutional Monarchy.

cards.title: The Rise of Absolute Monarchies
body: After the religious wars, the power of the monarchs was increased to achieve stable socio-economic conditions leading to the rise of Absolutism in the 17th C. Absolutism is a government system in which the ruler holds total power and a divine right to rule. Such rulers can make laws, impose taxes, lead the army and determine their own foreign policies

cards.title: France under Louis XIV (1661-1715)
body: Louis XIV rose to power in 1643 but he was only four years old thus power was given to Cardinal Mazarin, the chief minister who was able to crush the nobles who revolted against the monarchy.
Louis took over in 1661 after the death of Mazarin and desired to be the one and only ruler of France. He built a long-standing army of 400,000.
As the leader of the Bourbon dynasty, he tried to dominate European affairs by waging four wars from 1667-1713. He died in 1715 leaving France surrounded by enemies and in a great debt.

cards.title: Absolutism in Central and Eastern Europe – Prussia
body: Out of the 300 German states, the Prussian State emerged under Frederick William The Great Elector in the 17th C. it had the fourth largest army in Europe with 40,000 troops and a civil administration to levy taxes for the army.
The government officials were chosen from the Prussian aristocracy known as the Junkers who served as army officers. Frederick was replaced by his son King Frederick I.

cards.title: Austria
body: As one of the 300 German states, the Hapsburg dynasty of Austria had played a major role in the Holy Roman Empire E.g., Charles V. But after the Thirty Years War, they had lost their German Empire.
They later created the Austrian Empire in Eastern and Southeastern Europe in present day Austria, Czech Republic, and Hungary. They followed a less centralized absolute monarchy.

cards.title: Russia under Peter the Great
body: A new state emerged in the 15th C in Russia led by the Principality of Muscovy and its grand dukes. The first ruler was Ivan IV who was given the title Czar (Caesar) in 1533.

Ivan crushed the power of the Boyars (nobles) and expanded the Russian territories eastwards. The dynasty ended in 1598 putting Russia in a period of Anarchy (the absence of a government) known as the Times of Troubles.

The period of Anarchy ended with the election of Michael Romanov of the Romanov Dynasty as the new czar in 1613. The dynasty lasted until 1917; one famous leader was Peter the Great who rose to power in 1689.

Peter was an absolute monarch like his predecessors who ruled by dividing Russia into provinces. After visiting the west, he westernized Russia and modernized his army and navy, he also built the city of St. Petersburg, which remained as Russian capital until 1918.

lessons.title: The Development of Art and Political Thought

cards.title: A. Artistic Development
body: A new movement known as Mannerism emerged in Italy in the 1520s and 1530s replacing the Renaissance art, it used elongated figures.

In the 16th C, Mannerism was replaced by a new movement known as Baroque which begun in Italy and eventually spread into Europe and Latin America. The Baroque paintings had dramatic effects and rich details while, the architecture reflected the power of the leaders.

cards.title: B. Literature
body: 16th-17th C, a Cultural Flowering took place in England during the Elizabeth Era (1558-1603), where drama grew as the most popular form of literature. The remarkable works of William Shakespeare showed great language skills and knowledge of Human psychology.
Spanish literature also saw its golden age in this era as drama and novel writing flourished. The works of Miguel de Cervantes is an example.

cards.title: C, Political Thoughts
body: The English revolutions of the 17th C brought different ideas from two English thinkers:

Thomas Hobbs wrote Leviathan, a book dealing with political disorder because he was worried about the revolutionary disturbances in England. He believed that before social organization, human life was solitary, poor, nasty and short as humans were guided by a ruthless struggle for self-preservation instead of reason. Thus, absolute rule was needed to preserve order in the society and suppress rebellion.

John Locke wrote the Two Treatises of Government, in which he argued against Hobbs’s idea of the absolute rule of one person. Locke believed that before social organization, humans lived in a state of equality and freedom, but they needed governments to protect their rights based on a mutual obligation with in the state of nature. Locke supported the demands for Constitutional government, the rule of law and the protection of rights.
